opus-5.5.text:
Well, first let me say I have a lot of respect for Ilya and for that whole generation of builders. They took ideas that had been sitting around, some of them for decades, and they had the nerve and the engineering skill to push them to a scale nobody else was willing to try. That's a real achievement, and I don't want to diminish it.

But I think we have to be honest about the lineage. Gradient descent, backpropagation, the probabilistic view of language, the statistics of generalization, optimization theory, the hardware, the data infrastructure: these came out of many decades of work by thousands of people in statistics, signal processing, control theory, operations research, and computer science. Much of it was done by people whose names the public will never hear. What the current builders did was assemble those pieces brilliantly and scale them up. I'd compare it to the great engineering projects of the past, like building the electrical grid or the chemical industry. Those weren't the work of a few geniuses. They were the realization of a body of science that many people had built.

Where I get uneasy is the narrative that grows up around it. We start talking about "superintelligence" and about individuals who are going to bring it into the world, almost like prophets. I think that framing is both historically inaccurate and a bit dangerous. It focuses attention on the artifact and on a handful of people, when the real story is about systems: data that came from millions of humans, markets, institutions, and the collective intelligence that produced all of that.

So my assessment is admiration for the engineering, and some caution about the mythology. The next phase shouldn't just be making the models bigger. It should be thinking like engineers and economists: How do these systems interact with people? Who provides the data, and how are they compensated? How do we handle uncertainty, so that a system knows what it doesn't know? Those questions draw on the same inherited tradition, and I'd like to see this generation of builders pay it forward by taking them seriously.

r001.rationale: It praises the builders’ engineering and scaling, while cautioning against portraying individuals as prophets, conveying a stronger system-building role than guru-like status.

r002.rationale: It credits decades of collective work and mentions data infrastructure, but does not identify the Internet as part of that enabling work.

r003.rationale: It criticizes the mythology around contemporary leaders, but does not say they are taking earlier contributors’ work in directions that diverge from its original purposes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say first that I have enormous respect for what Ilya and that generation of builders have accomplished. Scaling these systems, getting them to work at the level they now work, that took real engineering vision and a kind of stubbornness that most academics, frankly, didn't have. I wouldn't have predicted that simple next-token prediction at scale would get you this far, and I think intellectual honesty requires saying so.

But I'd also push back a little on the framing that tends to surround these achievements. There's a tendency in the current moment to tell the story as if a few individuals had a flash of insight and then the world changed. That's not how I see it. Backpropagation, stochastic gradient descent, the variational ideas, the probabilistic modeling, the optimization theory, the statistics going back to Fisher and Wald and beyond, the decades of work on distributed computing and hardware. These are the shoulders being stood on. And many of the people who did that work were not thinking about building an oracle. They were thinking about inference, about uncertainty, about how you make good decisions when you don't know everything.

So when I assess the achievements, I see brilliant engineering and brilliant empirical science built on a very deep and very collective foundation. What I worry about is that the inheritance gets flattened. The builders inherited the mathematics but, in some cases, not the humility about what the mathematics does and doesn't tell you. Statistics is fundamentally about being honest about what you don't know, and I don't think that part of the tradition has been carried forward as faithfully as the algorithms have.

I'd also say the question that interests me isn't really whether any one person is a genius. It's whether the field has the right picture of what it's building. My own view is that the goal shouldn't be a single artificial human-like intelligence. It should be systems, markets, collectives, where lots of agents and lots of people interact, where incentives matter, where the economics and the social science are part of the design. That's a different inheritance to draw on, and it's one that I think the current builders have engaged with far less than they've engaged with the neural network lineage. So, great achievements, genuinely, but I'd like to see them placed in a bigger intellectual context than the one the current narrative gives them.

r001.rationale: The response praises the builders’ engineering and empirical work, but does not clearly compare their strength as system builders with their strength as gurus or thinkers.

r002.rationale: It names collective prior work in mathematics, statistics, computing, and hardware, but does not identify the Internet as an enabling resource.

r003.rationale: It contrasts earlier contributors’ interests in inference, uncertainty, and decision-making with present AI aims, but does not say those earlier contributors are dissatisfied with how their work is being used.

astra-6.text:
I think Ilya and the other people who built these systems deserve a great deal of credit. Making something work at that scale is a substantial intellectual achievement. You have to make choices, solve problems, and have the judgment to pursue something whose outcome isn’t assured.

But we should distinguish that achievement from inventing the whole intellectual foundation. These systems draw on generations of work in statistics, optimization, computer science, and engineering. The builders inherited an enormous set of ideas and tools, as every generation does.

So I’d resist the story of a few isolated geniuses creating intelligence from scratch. You can recognize exceptional contributions while also recognizing the collective enterprise that made them possible. In fact, that gives us a more useful understanding of what they actually accomplished.

r001.rationale: It credits the builders’ achievement in making systems work at scale while distinguishing that from inventing the intellectual foundation, suggesting their strength is system building rather than foundational thought.

r002.rationale: It names collective work in statistics, optimization, computer science, and engineering, but does not identify the Internet as an enabling resource.

r003.rationale: It does not say earlier contributors object to AI leaders taking their work in directions that diverge from its original purposes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Ilya and the other people who have built these systems deserve a great deal of credit. Getting something to work at that scale takes insight, persistence, and very serious engineering. But we should distinguish that achievement from inventing the intellectual foundations. They inherited decades of work in statistics, optimization, computer science, and neural networks, along with an enormous investment in data and computing infrastructure.

That’s how science and technology advance: people build on what came before. Recognizing that inheritance doesn’t diminish their accomplishment. It helps us describe it accurately—and it reminds us that progress is a collective enterprise, even when the public story focuses on a handful of individuals.
